name: NASHA Dx
question: Does transanal submucosal NASHA Dx injection improve fecal incontinence more than sham injection?

design.population: Adults aged 18–75 years with fecal incontinence for at least 12 months, CCFIS at least 10, at least four episodes over 2 weeks, and failed supervised conservative treatment.
design.description: Multicenter, double-blind, sham-controlled superiority randomized trial
design.locator: Full text, Methods—Patients and Randomisation, p 998; Figure 1; Mellgren 2014 full text, Materials and Methods—Patients

verdictNote: All three prespecified primary success criteria were met; 112/136 treated patients received a second injection.
takeaway: Transanal submucosal dextranomer in stabilized hyaluronic acid (NASHA Dx) produced more six-month fecal-incontinence responders than sham injection: 71/136 (52%) versus 22/70 (31%); odds ratio 2.36 (95% CI 1.24–4.47; P=0.0089). All three prespecified primary criteria were met.

reports.label: Six-month sham-controlled report
reports.citation: Graf W, Mellgren A, Matzel KE, et al. "Efficacy of dextranomer in stabilised hyaluronic acid for treatment of faecal incontinence: a randomised, sham-controlled trial." *Lancet.* 2011;377(9770):997-1003. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(10)62297-0
reports.followUp: Six-month masked assessment with a 2-week bowel diary
reports.followUpLocator: Full text, Methods—Procedures and Statistical analysis, pp 998–1000

results.endpoint: At least 50% reduction in fecal-incontinence episodes
results.note: Intention-to-treat with last observation carried forward; 132/136 active and 65/70 sham patients were assessed at six months. Modeled response was 52.7% (95% CI 39.8–65.2) versus 32.1% (20.2–46.9). Both six-month primary criteria were met: between-arm P<0.05 and active-arm lower 95% CI >35%.
results.locator: Full text, Methods—Statistical analysis, p 999; Results and Table 3, p 1000

results.endpoint: At least 25% reduction in fecal-incontinence episodes
results.measure: 12-month active-arm responder proportion, intention-to-treat with last observation carried forward
results.note: The third prespecified primary criterion required the lower 95% CI to exceed 50%; the sham arm was unmasked and excluded after six months.
results.locator: Full text, Methods—Procedures and primary endpoint, p 999; Results, Table 3, p 1000

results.measure: Mean increase from baseline at six months
results.note: Prespecified secondary endpoint; intention-to-treat with last observation carried forward.
results.locator: Full text, Methods—Secondary endpoints and Statistical analysis, pp 999–1000; Results, p 1000

harms.label: Common adverse events during the six-month blinded phase

values.exp: Proctalgia 19/136 (14.0%); injection-site bleeding 7/136 (5.1%); fever 11/136 (8.1%); rectal hemorrhage 10/136 (7.4%)
values.ctl: Proctalgia 2/70 (2.9%); injection-site bleeding 12/70 (17.1%); fever 0/70; rectal hemorrhage 1/70 (1.4%)

harms.note: Injection-site bleeding was transient and stopped without intervention; the paper did not report Clavien-Dindo grades.
harms.locator: Full text, Results and Table 4, p 1001

harms.label: Serious treatment-related adverse events during the six-month blinded phase

values.exp: Rectal abscess 1/136 (0.7%), surgically drained; prostatic abscess 1/136 (0.7%), treated with antibiotics

harms.note: There were 128 treatment-related events in the active arm and 29 in the sham arm; these are event counts, not patient counts.
harms.locator: Full text, Results and Table 4, p 1001

delivery.label: Injection technique and retreatment

values.exp: Outpatient anoscopic injection without anesthesia: 1 mL in each of four submucosal quadrants about 5 mm above the dentate line (4 mL initially; 4–8 mL total if repeated); 112/136 (82%) received a second injection at one month
values.ctl: Sham anoscopy without injection; 61/70 (87%) received a repeat sham procedure at one month

delivery.note: Cleansing enema before treatment; needle held for 10 seconds to limit backflow. Retreatment was offered for CCFIS ≥10 without persistent adverse effects.
delivery.locator: Full text, Methods—Procedures, p 999; Results, p 1000

reports.label: Three-year active-arm follow-up
reports.citation: Mellgren A, Matzel KE, Pollack J, et al. "Long-term efficacy of NASHA Dx injection therapy for treatment of fecal incontinence." *Neurogastroenterol Motil.* 2014;26(8):1087-1094. doi:10.1111/nmo.12360
reports.followUp: 36 months in the 136 originally assigned to NASHA Dx; no continued sham comparison
reports.followUpLocator: Full text, Materials and Methods—Patients; Results, Figure 1

results.endpoint: At least 50% reduction in fecal-incontinence episodes
results.measure: 36-month responder proportion, last observation carried forward
results.note: At 36 months, 112/136 had an assessment; complete-case response was 59% (n=112) and missing-as-failure response was 44.9% (n=136).

results.endpoint: Cleveland Clinic Florida Fecal Incontinence Score
results.note: Within-arm change among patients originally assigned to NASHA Dx.

harms.label: Early treatment-related anorectal events

values.exp: Proctalgia 19/136 (14.0%); injection-site bleeding 7/136 (5.1%); rectal abscess 1/136 (0.7%); prostatic abscess 1/136 (0.7%)

harms.locator: Full text, Results, Table 4 and adverse-events paragraph
harms.note: First 6 months; rectal abscess required surgery and prostatic abscess resolved with antibiotics.

harms.label: Treatment-related events after six months
harms.locator: Full text, Results, Table 4 and adverse-events paragraph
harms.note: Through 36 months; no additional treatment-related serious adverse events were reported.

delivery.label: Injection technique
delivery.value: Outpatient anoscopic injection without anesthesia: 1 mL NASHA Dx in each of four submucosal quadrants, about 5 mm above the dentate line; needle retained 10 seconds after injection.

delivery.label: Repeat treatment and retention
delivery.value: At one month, patients with CCFIS at least 10 and no persistent adverse effects were offered retreatment; 112/136 (82%) received a second injection and 112/136 (82%) completed the 36-month assessment.
